events.title: Molière in the Park presents: DON JUAN
events.description: Molière in the Park, Brooklyn's home for free world-class theater, invites you to experience legendary French playwright Molière’s most subversive play.Don Juan has abandoned Elvira, whom he seduced into breaking her vows and marrying him. Over the course of a single adventure-filled day, he and his loyal sidekick, Sganarelle, encounter many of the people Don Juan has betrayed. As he seduces women, defies social conventions, mocks religion, and revels in provocation, his appetite for transgression seems impossible to satisfy. Yet the signs are unmistakable: the walls are closing in.Will he truly repent? Or will he just pretend to, like so many around him, and continue down the same path to the bitter end?Translated by Stephen Wadsworth and directed by Drama Desk nominee Lucie Tiberghien, DON JUAN is one of Molière’s most thrilling and provocative masterpieces. A feverish descent from seduction to reckoning, the play blends comedy, tragedy, and the supernatural, pushing Molière’s exploration of hypocrisy and morality further than any of his other works.This free production will once again feature live original cello music by Drama Desk nominated composer Johnathan Moore.RSVPs are encouraged. Learn more at moliereinthepark.org/don-juan-2026

events.title: 250th 1776 Peace Conference Celebration
events.description: This living history event will commemorate the 250th Anniversary of the only Peace Conference held during the American Revolution on September 11th, 1776.Saturday, September 12th, 11 am to 4pm At Conference House & Park Great Lawn, 7455 Hylan Blvd, Tottenville SI 10307 $10.00 Each; Children under 12 $5.00,  children 5 years and under FREE.  ALL Scouts in uniform admitted for FREE and get a Conference House Patch! Outdoor Event. Opening Ceremony featuring the Staten Island Bagpipers at 11 am.The highlight of the event is a reading of an excerpt of the Peace Conference at 2pm. Board members portraying all of the key figures discussing the many issues that were faced back then, in an effort to put an end to the Revolutionary War. The day includes costumed Colonial dancers who are accompanied by 18th Century music.There will be an outdoor Museum exhibit and visitors can take a peek at the vegetables growing in the Colonial Kitchen Garden.Various 18th century craftspeople demonstrate Colonial era trades such as woodworking, coopering, tin smithing, black smithing beekeeping, chair caning, spinning, wampum making techniques and weaving and quilting. Visitors see demonstrations and learn about various crafts.Among other activities children have the opportunity to make kites (in homage to Ben Franklin) and to try their hand at the art of calligraphic writing. Colonial cooking is demonstrated at the outdoor open hearth fires by the dedicated members of the Conference House Auxiliary. They will share Colonial recipes for cornbread and soup. Modern day snacks will be available for purchase.

events.title: Docent led tours of the Historic Conference House Museum
events.description: Take a docent led tour of the Conference House Museum also known as the Billiopp House located on Staten Island, New York and overlooking the Raritan Bay. This two-story grand fieldstone house was built by powerful landowner Royal Navy Captain Christopher Billopp About 1680. He wanted a home that would be an expression of his massive wealth, as well as a symbol of the stability of the colonies.  Nearly a century later the Billopp House had become a center of colonial hospitality. Billopp’s great-grandson, loyal to the crown, offered his ancestral family home as the site of a meeting of great importance.It is Named The Conference House because it is the site of the only Peace Conference of the American Revolution. Continental Congress representatives Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and Edward Rutledge met here with British Admiral Lord Howe at his request on September 11,1776 in an unsuccessful effort to stop the American Revolution. The Americans had already written and signed the Declaration of Independence on July 4,1776 and their course would not be altered. Though the group discusses options for a peaceful cessation of hostilities, no agreement was reached and the fighting continued for seven years.Today the Conference House Museum presents an interpretation of an 18th century colonial manor to the general public. The building is owned by NYC Parks and operated by the Conference House Association as a historic house museum in partnership with the Historic Trust of NYC.

events.title: Jackie O and John Perreault at Snug Harbor: A Literary Portrait
events.description: Jackie O and John Perreault at Snug Harbor: A Literary Portrait Featuring guest speakers:   Wayne Koestenbaum, Author of Jackie Under My Skin and Andy Warhol: A Biography Daniel Rothbart, artist currently exhibiting at Snug Harbor and friend of John Perreault On the 50th anniversary of Snug Harbor opening its doors to the community after the transition from Sailors’ Snug Harbor into Snug Harbor Cultural Center on September 12, 1976, join us for an intimate literary reading that traces the legacies of two essential figures within the Snug Harbor story.  When: Saturday, September 12, 2026 |  3:00 PM – 5:00 PMWhere: Newhouse Center for Contemporary Art, Main Hall Gallery, Building CAdmission: Free (Registration Required) Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and John Perreault were each instrumental in shaping the story of Snug Harbor Cultural Center. In the mid-1970s, when after being saved from demolition, the former sailors’ home faced an uncertain future, Kennedy toured the site on behalf of the Municipal Art Society, lending her influence to the preservation effort. Later, she famously piloted the Staten Island Ferry back to Manhattan. A decade later, Perreault became one of the first professional curators at the Newhouse Center for Contemporary Art at Snug Harbor (1985–1989), where he championed Staten Island artists such as Julia Healy, Elizabeth Egbert, and Cynthia Mailman, while also presenting off-island figures including Nancy Spero, Judy Chicago, and Gillian Jagger. Though they moved in different circles, Andy Warhol forms a compelling link between them. As chief art critic for The Village Voice in the 1960s and ’70s, Perreault became a key chronicler of Pop Art and a close friend of Warhol—at one point speaking with him nightly for nearly two years. Warhol’s Jackie series, based on images of Kennedy  before and after the assassination, was among the works Perreault reviewed with particular attention. Jackie herself maintained a cordial relationship with Warhol and shared friends in New York’s art and fashion worlds, including Halston and Truman Capote. In the summer of 1972, she and her, Lee Radziwill, along with their children, stayed at Warhol’s Eothen estate in Montauk. Another point of resonance between Jackie O and John Perreault is fashion. Kennedy helped define 1960s style through the so-called “Camelot” look—pillbox hats, tailored shift dresses, and Oleg Cassini-designed suits—later evolving into her signature “Jackie O” ensemble of oversized sunglasses, headscarves, and Gucci handbags. Perrealut, in turn, approached fashion as an artistic medium. In 1969, with Hannah Weine and Eduardo Costa, he co-organized the Fashion Show Poetry Event, a hybrid of runway, performance, and text. Twenty artists designed garments worn by fellow artists and poets, accompanied by live music and recorded readings written specifically for each look. Participants included Andy Warhol, James Lee Byars, Alex Katz, Marisol, Claes Oldenburg, and James Rosenquist, among others.    Artist and writer Wayne Koestenbaum is the author of Jackie Under My Skin, a book about Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and Andy Warhol: A Biography. In 1998, he curated an exhibition titled Bathroom at the Thomas Healy Gallery, exploring themes of the body, voyeurism, and personal territory, which included work by John Perreault. Artist and writer Daniel Rothbart met Perreault in 1999, and the two maintained a close friendship and ongoing creative dialogue until Perreault’s death in 2015, frequently writing about one another’s work. Perreault included Rothbart in The Ritual Feast at KK Projects in New Orleans in 2008. Drawing on personal experience and longstanding engagement with their subjects, Koestenbaum and Rothbart will reflect on the intertwined legacies of Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and John Perreault, and consider how each helped shape the cultural history of Snug Harbor. This literary reading is part of our Serpentine Sybils public art exhibition on view at the Pond and the Glasshouse

events.title: Docent led tours of the Historic Conference House Museum
events.description: Take a docent led tour of the Conference House Museum also known as the Billiopp House located on Staten Island, New York and overlooking the Raritan Bay. This two-story grand fieldstone house was built by powerful landowner Royal Navy Captain Christopher Billopp About 1680. He wanted a home that would be an expression of his massive wealth, as well as a symbol of the stability of the colonies.  Nearly a century later the Billopp House had become a center of colonial hospitality. Billopp’s great-grandson, loyal to the crown, offered his ancestral family home as the site of a meeting of great importance.It is Named The Conference House because it is the site of the only Peace Conference of the American Revolution. Continental Congress representatives Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and Edward Rutledge met here with British Admiral Lord Howe at his request on September 11,1776 in an unsuccessful effort to stop the American Revolution. The Americans had already written and signed the Declaration of Independence on July 4,1776 and their course would not be altered. Though the group discusses options for a peaceful cessation of hostilities, no agreement was reached and the fighting continued for seven years.Today the Conference House Museum presents an interpretation of an 18th century colonial manor to the general public. The building is owned by NYC Parks and operated by the Conference House Association as a historic house museum in partnership with the Historic Trust of NYC.

events.title: Molière in the Park presents: DON JUAN
events.description: Molière in the Park, Brooklyn's home for free world-class theater, invites you to experience legendary French playwright Molière’s most subversive play.Don Juan has abandoned Elvira, whom he seduced into breaking her vows and marrying him. Over the course of a single adventure-filled day, he and his loyal sidekick, Sganarelle, encounter many of the people Don Juan has betrayed. As he seduces women, defies social conventions, mocks religion, and revels in provocation, his appetite for transgression seems impossible to satisfy. Yet the signs are unmistakable: the walls are closing in.Will he truly repent? Or will he just pretend to, like so many around him, and continue down the same path to the bitter end?Translated by Stephen Wadsworth and directed by Drama Desk nominee Lucie Tiberghien, DON JUAN is one of Molière’s most thrilling and provocative masterpieces. A feverish descent from seduction to reckoning, the play blends comedy, tragedy, and the supernatural, pushing Molière’s exploration of hypocrisy and morality further than any of his other works.This free production will once again feature live original cello music by Drama Desk nominated composer Johnathan Moore.RSVPs are encouraged. Learn more at moliereinthepark.org/don-juan-2026

events.description: Hart Island is the largest public cemetery in the country and has served New York City since 1869. While Hart Island is currently only used for city burials, the island is deeply connected to New York City institutions. events.title: Molière in the Park presents: DON JUAN
events.description: Molière in the Park, Brooklyn's home for free world-class theater, invites you to experience legendary French playwright Molière’s most subversive play.Don Juan has abandoned Elvira, whom he seduced into breaking her vows and marrying him. Over the course of a single adventure-filled day, he and his loyal sidekick, Sganarelle, encounter many of the people Don Juan has betrayed. As he seduces women, defies social conventions, mocks religion, and revels in provocation, his appetite for transgression seems impossible to satisfy. Yet the signs are unmistakable: the walls are closing in.Will he truly repent? Or will he just pretend to, like so many around him, and continue down the same path to the bitter end?Translated by Stephen Wadsworth and directed by Drama Desk nominee Lucie Tiberghien, DON JUAN is one of Molière’s most thrilling and provocative masterpieces. A feverish descent from seduction to reckoning, the play blends comedy, tragedy, and the supernatural, pushing Molière’s exploration of hypocrisy and morality further than any of his other works.This free production will once again feature live original cello music by Drama Desk nominated composer Johnathan Moore.RSVPs are encouraged. Learn more at moliereinthepark.org/don-juan-2026

events.title: Poetry at Bryant Park Reading Room
events.description: Chelsea Whitton is the author of Bear Trap (Dancing Girl Press, 2018) and Wonder Wheel, published by LSU Press in March of this year. She holds a PhD from the University of Cincinnati and an MFA in Poetry from The New School. Her poetry and prose have appeared in many of print and online publications, including Beloit Poetry Journal, Copper Nickel, Cream City Review, Poetry Ireland, The Atlanta Review, and Forklift-Ohio. Her work has been a finalist for the Gearhart Prize, and the Frost Place and Adrienne Richard awards for poetry. She is the recipient of the 2018 Sandy Crimmins National Poetry Prize. Raised in the Carolinas, she spent her twenties in New York and now lives in Southwestern Ohio, where she teaches at the Art Academy of Cincinnati.Dilruba “Ruba” Ahmed is the author of Bring Now the Angels (Pitt Poetry), with poems featured in New York Times Magazine, The Slowdown, and Poetry Unbound.  Her debut book, Dhaka Dust (Graywolf Press), won the Bakeless Prize.  Her poems have appeared in Kenyon Review, New England Review, Ploughshares, and Virginia Quarterly Review.  Her work has also been anthologized in Best American Poetry, Halal If You Hear Me, New Moons: Contemporary Writing by North American Muslims, They Rise Like a Wave: An Anthology of Asian American Women Poets, and elsewhere. Ahmed received The Florida Review’s Editors’ Award, a Dorothy Sargent Rosenberg Memorial Prize, and the Katharine Bakeless Nason Fellowship awarded by the Bread Loaf Writers Conference. events.title: Flamboyants! by La Compagnie Tilawcis, Musical Concert
events.description: A concert version of an original musical connecting the Creole cultures of Réunion Island, Puerto Rico, and New Orleans.Réunion Island-based theater company Tilawcis brings their latest work, Flamboyants!, on a North American tour this fall. This work of documentary theater with music explores the remarkable intersections of Creole culture and identity between the geographically distant communities of Réunion Island, New Orleans, and Puerto Rico through music, storytelling, and gorgeous projections.Five languages are spoken on stage, and nearly a dozen instruments are played, fusing maloya, bomba, and Mardi Gras Indians songs. The piece explores themes of memory, identity, resilience, connection, and cultural transmission through the prism of the Creole experience. It shines a light on the richness of Creole cultures and their capacity to overcome historical oppression.Flamboyants! is a philosophy as much as it is a work of theater. Despite the 10,000 miles that separate Réunion from New Orleans, the Creole languages spoken in those two places are close linguistic cousins. Maloya musicians use the same Canna indica seeds in their kayamb instrument (a rectangular rattle made of sugar cane tubes) as bomba musicians use to create maracas in Puerto Rico. While the ties between these cultures have long been lost, their ancient, resilient wisdom, connected by the African diaspora, once again finds a home on stage in the celebration of Creole identity that is Flamboyants!Plot Summary: Réunion Island. While a cyclone rages, a man curses his name before throwing himself in the Indian Ocean. He has no idea what repercussions this action will have on the other side of the world. From Puerto Rico to New Orleans, Creole peoples will unite to teach him his true history. A work of musical theater, documentary and fictional, even fantastical in certain moments, Flamboyants! asks us to interrogate what stories our own names carry, the ways we’re interconnected, and the cultural resilience of those who fight to not be forgotten.
